body.text: In short:
Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor Todd Russell has been remembered as a "man of quiet strength and deep loyalty".
He was farewelled at a funeral service in Launceston today, following his death from an illness last week.
Russell was thrown into national fame 20 years ago, after surviving two weeks underground in the mine.
Most of the world knew Todd Russell for his heroic emergence from the Beaconsfield mine, after two weeks spent buried beneath untold amounts of rubble.
But it was his fierceness on the football field, his larrikin sense of humour, and his hard-earned journey of personal growth that took centre stage at his funeral today.
Hundreds of people attended the ceremony in Launceston, following the 54-year-old's death last week after a battle with illness.
Russell was one of two miners who spent a fortnight trapped nearly a kilometre underground following the Beaconsfield mine collapse on Anzac Day in 2006.
The disaster killed miner Larry Knight, while Russell and Brant Webb were discovered after five days, trapped in a safety cage covered in rubble.
Their eventual rescue after two weeks under the rocks made headlines across the world and the two were thrust into the national media spotlight.
Journalist Fiona Reynolds, who gave the eulogy at the funeral, said she spoke to Russell recently about what should happen to his body after his death.
"He joked: 'I've been buried once and I didn't like that, so I thought I'd get burned next time and see what that's like',"
'More than a headline'
Ian Wheeler, who was friends with Russell for more than 30 years, said most Australians would always associate his mate with the Beaconsfield mine disaster.
"It was an extraordinary event that captured the attention of the nation and revealed something of Todd's resilience, courage and determination," Mr Wheeler said.
"But those that knew Todd best, knew he was much more than a headline or a chapter in Australia's history."
Mr Wheeler described Russell as a "man of quiet strength and deep loyalty" and said those who knew him would always remember his love for his family, his toughness, determination and larrikin humour.

"Those qualities captured the attention of the nation during the darkest days underground, but the truth is they were present long before that event and remain part of who he was long afterwards," he said.
Russell served on his local fire brigade up until February this year and was a passionate footballer and hunter.
Dr Reynolds said the former firefighter described himself as a "bit of a bastard" growing up, as he was "headstrong and stubborn".

She said the mine ordeal bonded him to some rescuers, but that media commitments and fame drove a wedge between himself and some he loved, with him speaking publicly about his mental health struggles.
"Fame cost him his privacy, his identity and Todd would have handed back the money that came with it for an ordinary life again," Dr Reynolds said.
"Toughness wasn't just physical for Todd, he wore it like an emotional shield."
A statement by Russell's wife Donna, who married him in hospital about six months ago, was read out during the funeral.
"We didn't get to finish our story, but every memory we made I hold onto it dearly because it shaped who I am," she wrote.
"You were my rock, the one who made me laugh when life got hard, who held me close when everything felt heavy."
'He turned things around'
Russell's relationship with his first wife, Carolyn, and their three children Trent, Maddison and Liam, was strained for large parts of his life.
Standing alongside his siblings, Liam Russell said that he and his father "didn't always see eye to eye" and that there were "times growing up where things weren't how they should have been".
"What matters just as much, if not more, was the effort to work on himself and his relationship with us kids — which I am eternally grateful for,"
"He turned things around. That takes something real. It takes effort, it takes reflection and it takes heart."
This sentiment was echoed by Russell's sister Lisa Scott, who said she "couldn't be prouder" of the man her brother became in his final years, even as he struggled with his health.
"He put in the work, he listened, he cared, he was kinder, he was more patient and more understanding, which saw him become the best version of himself I had ever known," Ms Scott said.
"To the world he is Todd Russell, the Beaconsfield mine disaster survivor, the footballer, the firefighter, the hunter — but to me, he'll always be my little brother."
Russell's coffin was given a guard of honour by Tasmania Fire Service (TFS) personnel upon its arrival at the funeral home and was loaded onto a TFS vehicle at the end of the ceremony.
Attendees at the funeral were asked to make donations to the Leukaemia Foundation instead of bringing flowers.
